title: Measured tones
hookLine: recite the Qur'an in slow, measured rhythm (73:4)

cards: Play a podcast at double speed and you'll get the information. You won't get the person. The pauses, the breath before a hard sentence, the way a voice slows down when it means something: all gone.
The same verse that calls the Prophet to stand the night tells him how to recite once he's standing. And the instruction uses one root twice, in a way that sounds like what it asks for.

teach.b: Verse four ends, in Pickthall's translation: "and chant the Qur'an in measure." The Arabic is wa rattili al-Qur'ana tartila. Rattil, and then tartil: the verb and its noun together, which in Arabic adds emphasis.
Recite it in measure, truly in measure.

teach.h: EVERY SOUND GETS ITS OWN ROOM.
teach.b: Tartil means a recitation that is slow, clear, evenly spaced, each letter given its full sound. How did the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ actually recite?

teach.h: LETTER BY LETTER, VERSE BY VERSE.
teach.b: His wife Umm Salamah was asked, and according to reports in Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, she described his recitation as distinct, letter by letter, pausing at the end of each verse.
And Anas ibn Malik, in Sahih al-Bukhari, said he would draw out the long vowels.

teach.h: TAJWID: THE SCIENCE OF THE MEASURE.
teach.b: From verses like this one grew an entire science, tajwid, the rules for pronouncing the Qur'an correctly: where to lengthen, where to pause, how each letter is formed. It is passed on from teacher to student.
Different reciting styles developed too, slower and more melodic, or plainer, but they share the measure. Why does it matter? Verse five gives a hint: We are about to send down on you a weighty word.
You don't carry something heavy at a run. You carry it slowly, with your full attention. Tartil is what attention sounds like out loud.
The slowness isn't a delay before the meaning. It's how the meaning gets in.

how: Muslims who learn to recite the Qur'an study tartil and the rules of tajwid with a teacher: slow, clear, with lengthened vowels and pauses at verse ends, in prayer and in daily reading.

games.q: you want to recite the way Umm Salamah described the Prophet's recitation. what do you do?
o: letter by letter, pausing at each verse.
games.why: she described it as distinct, letter by letter, with a pause at the end of each verse.

practice: Recite a short surah you know, al-Fatiha or al-Ikhlas, in Arabic or in translation, at half your usual speed, giving every word its full sound and pausing to breathe at the end of each verse.
If you don't know one, say any line you love the same way, a word at a time, as if each word were heavy. Then sit in the quiet after.

wordCard.voice: Tartil. Slow, clear, measured recitation, each letter given its room. In 73:4: rattili al-Qur'ana tartila, recite it in measure. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: measured, distinct recitation, from the root r-t-l; 73:4 says rattili al-Qur'ana tartila.

carryVoice: Your line: slowly, measured. Heavy things are carried at a walk, not a run. Day six hundred fifty-three, done.
